>> Live from "NPR News" in Washington, I'm Rylan Barton.
President Trump says he ordered the Justice Department lawsuit over Alaska's Senate race.
In an appearance with Florida, Governor Ron DeSantis Trump said his administration sued
to block certification of the election if his favored candidate incumbent Republican
Senator Dan Sullivan loses.
>> I'm the one that said do it.
They have two guys run named Dan Sullivan running.
So the Democrats put up a guy, never, I don't think he ever voted before, all of a sudden
he decides to run.
>> An unaffiliated candidate with the same name is on the ballot, along with Democrat
Mary Peltola, the Alaska Supreme Court previously rejected efforts to remove the other Sullivan.
The lawsuit has sparked concerns about a lengthy battle between the U.S. government and states
over the election certification.
Official agents spotted outside a polling place in Tallahassee, Florida this week have raised
concerns about voter intimidation and government interference.
But as Regan McCarthy of Member Station WFSU reports, officials say the agents were just
trying to vote.
>> U.S. Customs and Border Protection say the agents were on their way out of the state
when they stopped at the polling site.
When they realized they couldn't vote, they left.
Leon County election supervisor Mark Early says he believes this was an isolated incident.
>> The emotional level in our country, you know, just the appearance makes everybody
jump to conclusions.
And I wish everybody to take a breath, you know, look at what's really happening.
It's safe to go out to the polls.
>> Another election supervisor in South Florida says she's investigating a traffic stop by
agents near an early voting site this week.
The U.S. Justice Department plans to send 1,000 observers to polling places around the
country on election day.
For NPR News, I'm Regan McCarthy in Tallahassee.
>> A bipartisan group of lawmakers is urging the Pentagon to immediately restore Ukraine's
access to the SpaceX star shield satellite Internet system used to intercept Russian
drones.
Today, President Trump brushed off questions about the role SpaceX CEO Elon Musk played
in the disruptions.
Alexander Ward of the Wall Street Journal told NPR's Here and Now it's unclear who ordered
the service to be throttled.
Musk says the White House gave some sort of directive, implicit or explicit, to Musk to
do this.
The White House says Elon acted on his own and now they're sort of working it out, but
that Elon also has the ability to do this because it's a private company.
But then the administration's messaging on this kind of changed yesterday.
Not only just Trump calling Musk to unthrottle the system, but you also had Vice President
J.D.
Vance say, look, you know, Musk wouldn't have done this without some sort of input from
the U.S.
Government.
There's still a big mystery out there as to did Musk go rogue or was there some sort of
still White House green light?
Alex Ward from the Wall Street Journal reporting major U.S. stock indexes fell today as the
market came under increasing pressure from rising oil prices.
The S&P 500 lost more than half a percent.
The Dow fell nearly one and a quarter percent.
This is NPR.
A new defense technology company plans to use gene editing and cloning to create super
dogs for military and police use.
The company called Warhound just got $200 million in funding, NPR's John Ruich reports.
The company says it plans to rebuild America's domestic supply of elite working dogs for
the military, law enforcement and first responders.
It will use colossal biosciences, gene editing tools and cloning technology to produce healthier
dogs with, quote, characteristics suited to demanding missions.
It will also use defense tech from the company Andoril to give dogs and their handlers better
awareness and protection in the field.
In a statement, the Texas-based company says animal welfare is central to the program.
The technology will make the dogs healthier and more durable and limit washouts.
John Ruich, NPR News.
The Pentagon has released a new set of UFO files, NPR's Jeff Brumfield reports they include
a recent sighting.
"In June, two FBI agents at an undisclosed facility spotted a black triangular object
several miles to the west of an observation post they were manning.
It rose up over a ridgeline, hovered for several seconds and then shot into a nearby canyon
at the speed of a fighter jet before disappearing into the shadows.
The report says the unidentified craft was silent and thermal imagery didn't show any
signs of engine exhaust.
In recent years, the government has become increasingly concerned about sighting some
possible Chinese drones around U.S. bases and research sites.
The origin of this specific object remains unknown, but the truth is out there."
Jeff Brumfield, NPR News.
This is NPR.
